question_text: Choose the correct sentence with parallel structure:

options.text: The candidate is hardworking, intelligent, and has sincerity.
The candidate is hardworking, intelligent, and sincere.
The candidate is hardworking, has intelligence, and sincere.
The candidate works hard, intelligent, and sincere.

hint_ladder.title: Spot the Pattern
hint_ladder.text: Think of a list like a train—each car should be the same type. Here, the sentence lists qualities about the candidate. What part of speech are they all supposed to be?

hint_ladder.title: The Golden Rule of Lists
hint_ladder.text: In a series, every item must match in grammatical form. If the first quality is an adjective (like 'hardworking'), the rest must also be adjectives. No mixing adjectives with verbs or nouns.

hint_ladder.title: Test Each Option
hint_ladder.text: Read each option aloud and listen for the 'rhythm.' Option A has two adjectives then a verb phrase ('has sincerity'). Option C jumps from adjective to verb phrase back to adjective. Option D starts with a verb phrase then switches to adjectives. Only one option keeps the same form all the way through.

hint_ladder.title: Find the Smooth Flow
hint_ladder.text: The correct answer uses three adjectives in a row: 'hardworking, intelligent, and sincere.' No extra verbs, no switching forms. It just flows naturally.

A.text: This one starts strong with two adjectives ('hardworking,' 'intelligent'), but then it switches to a verb phrase ('has sincerity'). It's like wearing sneakers with a formal suit—the pieces don't match. A smart test-taker might pick this because it sounds okay, but the 'has' breaks the pattern.

B.text: This is the one. All three items are adjectives: 'hardworking,' 'intelligent,' 'sincere.' They match perfectly, creating a smooth, balanced sentence. No awkward shifts, no extra words.

C.text: This option is a mix-up: it starts with an adjective ('hardworking'), then jumps to a verb phrase ('has intelligence'), then back to an adjective ('sincere'). It's like changing dance moves mid-song—confusing and off-beat. You might choose this if you focus on meaning over form, but grammar demands consistency.

D.text: Here, the first item is a verb phrase ('works hard'), but the next two are adjectives ('intelligent,' 'sincere'). The mismatch is obvious when you read it aloud. A common mistake is to think 'works hard' is just another description, but it's a different grammatical creature.

next_time_rule: When you see a list in a sentence, do the 'Same Form Check.' Ask yourself: Are all items the same part of speech? If the first is an adjective, the rest must be adjectives. If the first is a noun, all must be nouns. Keep the train cars identical.
deconstruct_text:
Let's break this down together. The sentence is describing the candidate using a list of qualities. For the list to be grammatically parallel, every item in that list must take the same form. Think of it like a team uniform—everyone wears the same jersey.

Option B is the only one where all three items are adjectives: 'hardworking,' 'intelligent,' and 'sincere.' They all describe the candidate directly and smoothly.

Now look at the others. Option A has two adjectives but then switches to a verb phrase ('has sincerity'). Option C mixes an adjective, a verb phrase, and another adjective. Option D starts with a verb phrase ('works hard') and then uses adjectives. Each of these breaks the parallel structure because the forms don't match.

Here's a mental trick for exam day: Read the list aloud and listen for the 'rhythm.' If it feels clunky or you have to change your tone mid-list, it's probably not parallel. Another trick is to strip the list down to just the items and see if they all look alike. For example, 'hardworking, intelligent, sincere'—all end in a similar descriptive way. But 'hardworking, intelligent, has sincerity'—that last one sticks out like a sore thumb.

So remember: parallel structure is all about consistency. Keep every item in the same grammatical form, and you'll never get tripped up.
